288.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (1 of 7)
288.hook: a ship in a storm, a monk on the shore, and a lump of clay with Krishna inside
288.carry: two, and the space between is love
288.tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (2 of 7)
288.howItsDone: Followers of Madhva, the Madhva Vaishnavas, centered on Udupi in Karnataka, worship Krishna as Vishnu, study Madhva's commentaries, and understand the soul as eternally distinct from and dependent on God.

segments.voice: Last week: Advaita, and the line not two. Clay and pots, the rope and the snake, and Shankara singing worship Govinda. Today, the teachers who read the same texts and said: two.

A trading ship is caught in a storm off the coast of Karnataka, near Udupi. A monk standing on the beach, the story goes, waves his cloth, and the ship comes safely in. The grateful captain offers him anything on board. The monk asks for one thing: a big lump of pale clay the sailors had been using as ballast. They break it open, and inside is an image of Krishna, holding a churning rope. That image, tradition says, is the one still worshiped in the Krishna temple at Udupi today. The monk was Madhva.
screen: `A SHIP IN A STORM OFF UDUPI.` → `A LUMP OF BALLAST CLAY.` → `KRISHNA INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Tradition places Madhva in the thirteenth century. He founded a school of Vedanta called Tattvavada, the teaching of what's real. Today it's usually called Dvaita: two. Where Shankara said not two, Madhva said two, clearly and forever. God is one reality. You are another. The world is another, and it's real, not a snake on a rope. Madhva spelled out five differences that never go away: God from souls, God from matter, each soul from every other soul, souls from matter, and each bit of matter from every other. Then the heart of it. God, for Madhva, is Vishnu, and only God is independent. Everything else, you, me, the ocean, the clay, depends on God, moment by moment. Not as a snake depends on a rope, a mistake. As a child depends on a parent: really there, really held. And here's what that gives devotion. Madhva's followers put it this way: if you and God were finally one, love would be only a stage on the way. Advaitins answer that differently, as you heard. For Madhva, the difference is the truth, so the love can last. Even a freed soul doesn't dissolve into God. It stays itself, in God's presence, loving and serving. The lover and the beloved stay two, and the space between them isn't a wall. It's where the love happens: two, and the space between is love. Advaita and Dvaita are both alive today, and neither is ranked here.
screen: `TATTVAVADA: WHAT'S REAL.` · `FIVE DIFFERENCES, FOREVER.` · `ONLY GOD IS INDEPENDENT.` · `FREED, AND STILL TWO.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love who is really, stubbornly not you: they laugh at different things, want different things. Notice that the love lives exactly in that difference; if they were you, there'd be no one to love. Feel the space between you as room, not distance. If you pray, turn that same warmth toward God, as other than you, and near.
Dvaita, two. God, souls and the world are really distinct, only God is independent, and the freed soul stays itself, loving God forever.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. A real God, a real you, and room between. Day two eighty-eight, done.

289.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (2 of 7)
289.hook: a teacher gives him a secret mantra; he climbs the temple tower and shouts it to the town
289.carry: two, and the space between is love
289.tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (3 of 7)
289.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas, followers of Ramanuja, worship Vishnu with Lakshmi, especially at temples like Srirangam, recite the Alvars' Tamil hymns alongside Sanskrit texts, and practice prapatti, surrender to God, as the heart of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Madhva's Dvaita, the Krishna in the ballast clay, and two, forever. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, a third answer, from a teacher who came before Madhva.

A young scholar named Ramanuja walks, tradition says, eighteen times to the house of an old teacher, asking for a sacred mantra. South India, around nine hundred years ago. Seventeen times he's turned away. The eighteenth time, the teacher gives it, with a warning: keep this secret. Tell no one, or you'll go to hell. Ramanuja walks straight to the temple, climbs the tall gateway tower, and calls the mantra out to everyone in the street below. The teacher is furious. Ramanuja says: if I go to hell and all these people are saved, I'll gladly go.
screen: `EIGHTEEN WALKS TO A TEACHER.` → `KEEP THIS SECRET.` → `SHOUTED FROM THE TEMPLE TOWER.`

segments.voice: The teacher, the story goes, embraced him. Ramanuja became the great teacher of the Sri Vaishnava tradition, centered at the temple of Srirangam, and he gave Vedanta a third answer. Not Shankara's not two. Not quite Madhva's two, which came about a century later. His school is called Vishishtadvaita: not two, but qualified. One reality, with real distinctions inside it. His picture is the body and the soul. You, the self, live in your body, guide it, and are the reason it moves. The body is real, not a snake on a rope. But it isn't independent either. It's yours. For Ramanuja, the whole universe, every soul and every grain of matter, is the body of God. And God, Vishnu, Narayana, is the soul of it all. He found this in the Upanishads, where the sage Yajnavalkya describes the inner controller. Paraphrased: the one who dwells in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who guides the earth from within: that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. For Ramanuja, you're really you, forever. God is really God. And yet God is closer to you than your own body is. That's why his tradition sees love and surrender to God as the path. The freed soul doesn't vanish into God. It enjoys God, as God's own. And the mantra from the tower? The tradition still teaches it openly.

segments.voice: Feel your body from the inside: your hands, your chest rising, the weight of your legs, really yours. Then try Ramanuja's picture: the room, the city, the trees, the people you love, all one great body, with a life at its center that lives in you too. If you pray, rest in that nearness; if not, feel the body and the room, and breathe.
Vishishtadvaita, not two but qualified. One reality: the world and souls are God's body, God is their inner self, and the soul stays itself, loving God.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Really you, really God, and very near. That's two eighty-nine.

290.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (3 of 7)
290.hook: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar
290.carry: two, and the space between is love
290.tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (4 of 7)
290.howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional traditions, teachers often explain that bhakti depends on the relationship between the devotee and God, and the gopis' love for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana is held up as its model.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishishtadvaita: Ramanuja on the temple tower, and the world as God's body. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, the question underneath all of this.

In Calcutta, the mystic Ramakrishna, whose student Vivekananda you met a few weeks ago, used to repeat a line from an old Bengali devotional song. People asked him about merging into God, becoming one with the absolute, and he'd answer, more or less: I don't want to become sugar. I want to taste sugar. It's a joke, and an argument. If you become the sugar, who's left to enjoy the sweetness?
screen: `CALCUTTA, RAMAKRISHNA.` → `I DON'T WANT TO BECOME SUGAR.` → `I WANT TO TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: The devotional schools make their case in that one line. Love, they say, needs two: a lover and a beloved, someone to give and someone to receive, someone to sing and someone to hear. Take away the difference, and you may have peace, or bliss, but not love the way a mother loves a child, or a friend a friend. The Bhagavata Purana tells a story about this. Krishna has left the village where he grew up, and the cowherd women who loved him, the gopis, are heartbroken. He sends his friend Uddhava, a learned man, to comfort them, and Uddhava comforts them with philosophy. Krishna is everywhere, he says; he's the self of all; you're never really apart from him. The gopis answer, paraphrased: that's lovely. We want Krishna. Not the self of all. Him. His flute, his laugh, his face. Uddhava, humbled, says he'd gladly be a bush or a creeper in their village, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. Other teachers explored the ground between. Nimbarka taught difference and non-difference at once. In Bengal, Chaitanya's followers called it inconceivable: one with God and different from God, both, beyond what the mind can hold. Now, fairly. Advaita teachers honor devotion too, as you heard with Bhaja Govindam, and some of them say love, fully ripened, dissolves into oneness. The devotional schools say love, fully ripened, stays two and grows forever. Hindus hold both, side by side. Nobody here has to pick.
screen: `LOVE NEEDS TWO.` · `THE GOPIS WANT KRISHNA, NOT A THEORY.` · `ONE AND DIFFERENT, BEYOND THOUGHT.` · `TWO VIEWS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Taste something, if it's nearby: a sip of tea, a raisin, a square of chocolate; if not, remember one. Let it sit on the tongue, and notice two things, the sweetness and the one enjoying it. If you pray, let that enjoyment turn toward God, the way Ramakrishna meant it.
Gopis, the cowherd women who loved Krishna. Love needs a lover and a beloved; to taste sugar, you can't become it.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Someone has to be there to taste it. Until tomorrow.

291.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (4 of 7)
291.hook: a shepherd poet isn't let into the temple, so he sings from behind the wall
291.carry: two, and the space between is love
291.tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (5 of 7)
291.howItsDone: At the Udupi Krishna temple, devotees view Krishna through a small latticed window, and Kanaka's window on the west wall is honored as a place of pilgrimage; the Haridasa songs of Kanakadasa and Purandaradasa are sung across Karnataka and in Carnatic music.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gopis, who wanted Krishna, not a theory, and Ramakrishna's sugar: taste it, don't become it. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, back to Udupi.

Visit the Krishna temple at Udupi today, the one with the image from the ballast clay, and you'll notice something odd. You don't see Krishna face to face through a big open doorway. You look at him through a small latticed window, nine little openings in a silver frame. And on the outside of the temple wall, on the west side, there's another window with a story attached, and a shrine to a poet. The story is about a shepherd who wasn't allowed in.
screen: `THE KRISHNA TEMPLE AT UDUPI.` → `SEEN THROUGH A SMALL WINDOW.` → `A SHEPHERD WHO WASN'T LET IN.`

segments.voice: His name was Kanakadasa, a poet from the Kuruba community, shepherds, in Karnataka. He belonged to the Haridasas, the servants of Hari, who took Madhva's teaching out of Sanskrit and into Kannada songs people could sing in the fields. His teacher, the Madhva scholar Vyasatirtha, is remembered as loving him. But when Kanaka came to Udupi to see Krishna, the temple authorities of the time, the story goes, wouldn't let him in because of his birth. So he went around to the back, stood outside the west wall, and sang, and sang, to a Krishna he couldn't see. Tradition says the wall cracked open, and the image inside turned around to face him. The crack became a window, still called Kanaka's window, and the image, they say, faces west to this day. Look at what the story does with Dvaita's line. The lover outside, the beloved inside, and between them not even a loving space: a hard, unfair wall. And the beloved turns. The difference doesn't close; Kanaka is still Kanaka, Krishna still Krishna. But the space becomes a window. There's a gentler story about him too. His teacher gave each student a banana and said: eat it where no one can see you. Everyone came back having eaten theirs in some hidden corner. Kanaka came back with his uneaten. Wherever I went, he said, Krishna was watching. For the Dvaita tradition, that's the relationship: two, always, and never out of sight.
screen: `THE HARIDASAS SANG IN KANNADA.` · `KEPT OUT, HE SANG FROM THE WALL.` · `THE IMAGE TURNED TO FACE HIM.` · `NEVER OUT OF SIGHT.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself outside a wall, the way Kanaka stood: maybe a real place where you felt unwelcome, maybe just the sense that God, or meaning, is somewhere you can't see. Sing inwardly, or just long, and picture a small window opening, and something on the other side turning toward you. If you pray, speak through that window; if not, stay by the wall, unhurried.
Kanakana kindi, Kanaka's window. A shepherd poet of Madhva's tradition kept outside the temple, and a Krishna who, the story says, turned to face him through it.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Even a wall can become a window. Day two ninety-one.

292.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (5 of 7)
292.hook: a baby monkey clings to its mother, a kitten is carried in its mother's mouth, and Ramanuja's followers asked which one you are
292.carry: two, and the space between is love
292.tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (6 of 7): Madhva and the five differences
292.howItsDone: Many Sri Vaishnavas formally take refuge through a rite called samashrayana, given by a teacher, and recite the dvaya mantra and Gita 18.66 daily; the northern (Vadakalai) and southern (Tenkalai) lineages are often told apart by the shape of the namam, the mark worn on the forehead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanakana kindi, Kanaka's window: the shepherd poet outside the wall at Udupi, and a Krishna who, the story says, turned to face him. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, back to Ramanuja's people.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: A mother monkey leaps from branch to branch. Her baby rides along, holding on to her belly with its own small hands. A mother cat moves her kitten another way. She picks it up by the scruff of its neck, and the kitten just hangs there, loose, carried. Two babies, two mothers, two ways of getting across. In South India, Ramanuja's later followers argued over these two animals, because the question underneath them is a big one. When God saves a soul, how much does the soul hold on?
screen: `A BABY MONKEY CLINGS.` → `A KITTEN IS CARRIED.` → `HOW MUCH DOES THE SOUL HOLD ON?`

segments.voice: You met Ramanuja a few days ago, on the temple tower, with the world as God's body. Today, the heart of how his followers practice: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge. Not giving up. Turning to God the way a child turns to a parent, and letting yourself be held. Sri Vaishnavas say Ramanuja himself, at the temple of Srirangam, offered a prose prayer of surrender before Vishnu and Lakshmi, and they still recite it. They treasure a verse near the end of the Gita, which they call the final verse. Krishna says, roughly: let go of every other support, take refuge in me alone, I will free you from every wrong, do not grieve. Later came the question from the hook. One lineage, later called the northern school, taught with the baby monkey: grace carries you, and you also hold on, with your own small effort. The other, the southern school, taught with the kitten: grace does everything, and even your holding on is a gift. Both lineages trace themselves to Ramanuja, and both are alive today. This path doesn't settle it. But both pictures share something: a mother and a child. Two. Surrender only makes sense if there's someone to surrender to. Advaita would say that in the end there's only one. Ramanuja's people say the soul is held, forever, and never stops being the one who is held. That's devotion needing difference. You can't be carried by yourself.
screen: `PRAPATTI: TAKING REFUGE.` · `TAKE REFUGE IN ME ALONE. DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `THE MONKEY HOLDS ON. THE KITTEN IS CARRIED.` · `BOTH TRACE THEMSELVES TO RAMANUJA.` · then, large: `YOU CAN'T BE CARRIED BY YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Feel the chair or the floor under you: you aren't holding yourself up right now, something else is. Notice one small effort you're still making, a tight jaw, a held breath, and let it go; you don't have to decide whether you're the monkey or the kitten, just notice what it feels like to be held. If you pray, name one worry and leave it with God for these few minutes.
Prapatti, taking refuge, the way of Ramanuja's followers. Clinging like a monkey or carried like a kitten, there is always a mother and a child. Two.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Held, and still yourself. Two ninety-two, done.

293.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (6 of 7)
293.hook: a devotee is kept outside a temple wall, and the story says the image of Krishna turned around to face him
293.carry: two, and the space between is love

293.howItsDone: Followers of Madhva, often called Madhvas, worship Vishnu as supreme; the Krishna temple at Udupi, which tradition says Madhva founded, is a center of their tradition, and pilgrims still look through Kanaka's window.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prapatti, taking refuge: the baby monkey and the kitten, both held. Today, back to Madhva.

Inside the Krishna temple at Udupi, the image faces west, toward a small window in the back wall. Two days ago you stood outside that wall with Kanakadasa, the shepherd poet kept out because of his birth, who sang until, the story says, the wall cracked and Krishna turned around to face him. Today, step inside, to the teacher who, tradition says, set that image there: Madhva. A God who turns toward someone on the far side of a wall is close to the heart of what he taught.
screen: `AN IMAGE FACING WEST.` → `A POET OUTSIDE THE WALL.` → `THE TEACHER WHO SET IT THERE.`

segments.voice: Five days ago you met Madhva's five differences: God, souls and the world, real and distinct forever. Today, the reason underneath them. Madhva sorts everything that is into two kinds. One is svatantra, independent, depending on nothing. Only God, Vishnu, is that. Everything else is paratantra, dependent: every soul, all of matter, even the goddess Lakshmi, his tradition says. All of it is real, and all of it leans on God. His followers sum it up in a phrase: Hari sarvottama, Vishnu is supreme. Now watch what Madhva's school does with a famous line. In the same chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad where Uddalaka taught his son with clay, the father says again and again: tat tvam asi, you are that. Advaita hears the self and Brahman as not two. Some teachers of his school hear tasya tvam asi, you are his: you belong to that. Others divide the sounds differently and hear atat tvam asi, you are not that. Same Sanskrit, a different ear. For Madhva, if the soul were secretly God, worship would be a kind of pretending. If God is truly other, and the soul truly depends on him, then love has somewhere to go. Back to the window: the story says God turned toward the poet. It isn't a lesson in philosophy, but it has the same shape: a real distance, and a love that crosses it. Advaita teachers would say the distance is finally unreal. Madhva's followers say it's where love lives. Both are Hindu, and both are still taught.
screen: `ONLY GOD IS INDEPENDENT: SVATANTRA.` · `TAT TVAM ASI, HEARD ANOTHER WAY.` · `IF GOD IS OTHER, LOVE HAS A PLACE TO GO.` · `A REAL DISTANCE, AND A LOVE THAT CROSSES IT.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let yourself feel small for a moment, in a good way: not ashamed, just small, the way you feel under a big sky, with so much bigger than you, the day ahead, the people you love, whatever holds it all. Let the distance be fine; Kanakadasa sang from outside the wall. If you pray, turn toward God from exactly where you are; if you don't, face toward something larger, and rest.
Svatantra, independent, depending on nothing. Only God is svatantra; souls and the world are real, different, and depend on him. The distance isn't a problem to solve. It's where love goes.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Only God stands on nothing; everything else leans on him. That's day two ninety-three.

294.title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (7 of 7)
294.hook: a hymn credited to the teacher of not two says the wave belongs to the ocean, never the ocean to the wave
294.carry: two, and the space between is love
294.howItsDone: Hindu schools of Vedanta, including Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita and the schools of Chaitanya and Vallabha, are all still taught in monasteries and lineages today, and many Hindus draw on more than one without choosing sides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, svatantra: only God is independent, and a poet outside a temple wall. Today, the last of these two weeks.
screen: `A REAL DISTANCE, AND A LOVE THAT CROSSES IT.`

segments.voice: Stand at the edge of the sea and watch one wave come in. It rises with its own shape, its own curl of foam, then slides back into the water. Was it ever separate from the ocean? Not really. Was it the whole ocean? Not quite either. A short hymn traditionally credited to Shankara, the great teacher of not two, uses exactly that picture. Not to win an argument. To pray. And in one line it holds both ends of these two weeks.
screen: `ONE WAVE COMES IN.` → `SEPARATE FROM THE OCEAN?` → `A HYMN FROM THE TEACHER OF NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: The hymn is called the Shatpadi, six verses, and its third verse says, paraphrased: even when difference is gone, Lord, I am yours; you are not mine. The wave belongs to the ocean. The ocean never belongs to the wave. Even here, a lover and a beloved: the point Ramakrishna made with sugar on day two hundred ninety: devotion needs someone to love and someone loved. Look back: you've walked a real map. Shankara's Advaita: not two. When the light comes on, the snake was only ever the rope, and your deepest self and Brahman, the ultimate reality, are one. Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita: one God, with the world and every soul as his body. Close enough to belong, distinct enough to love. Madhva's Dvaita: God, souls and world, real and different forever, and love crossing the distance. And there's more beyond them, which is why the week is called Dvaita and beyond. Chaitanya, in Bengal, taught that God and the soul are one and different at once, beyond what any mind can grasp: inconceivable oneness and difference, his followers call it. Vallabha, in the north, taught a pure non-dualism in which God's grace is everything. These teachers disagreed, sharply, for centuries, in books and debates. And the tradition kept all of them. Hindus today walk each of these roads, and many borrow from more than one. Even Advaita sings: hymns to the goddess, to Shiva and to Krishna are traditionally credited to Shankara himself. This path doesn't pick a winner. It shows you the map, and leaves room for the wave.
screen: `THE WAVE BELONGS TO THE OCEAN.` ·`SHANKARA: NOT TWO.` · `RAMANUJA: ONE, WITH DISTINCTIONS.` · `MADHVA: TWO, FOREVER.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Breathe in: not two, everything one field, you and the room and the sky. Breathe out: two, yourself facing something larger, the way you'd face a person you love. Go back and forth a few times, then let whichever feels like home stay; there's no wrong answer, and if you pray, rest in whichever way you pray.

Shatpadi, the six-verse hymn where even Shankara, teacher of not two, keeps a lover and a beloved. Madhva's two, Ramanuja's one with distinctions, Chaitanya's one and different at once: all of them keep room for love.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. The wave is still a wave, and still the ocean's. Two weeks, done; see you tomorrow.
